ball

All three take the cap that already exists: the neck stops scaling with the ball and the aperture plane moves instead. Small pays for that — its mouth is 72 % of its diameter, so it loses the top of the picture.

shell

Outward puts the relief on the face you look at — the verdict the printed pair gave. Both walls attenuate identically, so lit in the dark they transmit the same picture; in a lit room the outward shell also catches light on the relief.

picture

Reflected puts the picture on twice, each copy the mirror of its neighbour, so both joins are mirror lines. Wrapped runs it once around the whole ball.

The bottom carries the painting's centre, projected stereographically onto the south cap — the one view a latitude band can never give you, because looking up at a hanging ball you are looking straight at the pole.

Limits the wall by both faces at once, so outward and inward carry the same wall to the micron. Makes a worse ornament and the only honest dark-room comparison.

view

The preview is decimated so it can be rebuilt while a control moves, which makes it read smoother than the object is. Drag right to see the real thing. Nothing else changes: the readouts and the STL are full resolution at every setting.

Beer–Lambert through the wall, unrolled: colatitude down, longitude across. This is the picture the ball makes, and it is not the heightfield — the map is exponential, so the thin end spreads and the thick end crushes.

printing it

Ball: 0.12 mm layers, 8 wall loops, 0.40 mm line width, 100 % infill, supports OFF, 5 mm outer brim, elephant-foot compensation 0.20 mm — the first layer is the sealing rim and the mouth of the bayonet bore. Print as exported, rim on the bed.

Cap: a different recipe — 0.16 mm layers, 4 wall loops, 25 % gyroid, minimum layer time 10 s, fan 100 %, 5 mm brim, supports off, spigot down.

To close it: push the cap in, then turn it counter-clockwise seen from above through about 52° to a hard stop. It is a one-way run; the wrong way jams after 6°.

about this build

A JavaScript port of xmas3.py's spherical path. Verified field by field against the Python on identical decoded pixels: 1.3e-13 mm at small, 3.4e-13 at medium, and every vertex and face of the mesh bit-identical. The exported medium ball matches the one that was actually printed to 0.001 % by volume, and the real cap seats, twists and locks in it.

The booleans run on manifold-3d in WebAssembly — the same library the Python uses, so the CSG is the same algorithm rather than two that agree by luck.

Everything runs in this page. No upload, no server, no network.

The sphere is the open question at the end of From Panel to Cylinder — no rectangle maps to it without distortion, and the overhang argument that governs the column gets worse near the equator. This page is that question answered and printed. painting2lamp is the same idea on a cylinder, and the build guide is where the heightfield comes from.
